h1: The 8 Best Immersion Blenders Under $100 for Soups, Sauces and Smoothies, Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 immersion blenders under $100 compared on motor wattage, speed control, attachments and build, from Braun to KitchenAid.
summary: The Braun MultiQuick 7 is the immersion blender to buy under $100 if you will use the extra food processor attachment, while the Braun Vario 5 gives you 500W and 21 speeds with fewer parts. The Turelar 1100W set is the cheapest way to get a bundle of attachments, and the KitchenAid is a solid mid-priced all-rounder.
intro: Wattage is the number everyone compares and it is the least useful one. A 1100W label looks impressive, but a stick blender lives or dies by blade design, shaft length and how well the speed control lets you start gently. Splatter across the backsplash is the real test of a hand blender, and bigger watts do not fix it.

This ranking looks at eight immersion blenders in the under $100 range. We reviewed their listings and published specs for motor power, speed settings, attachments and build, and we flag where a listing gives little detail. We do not claim to have run any of them through a soup pot.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 7 3-in-1 Immersion Blender and Food Processor
products.verdict: A Braun stick blender that adds a food processor attachment for the price of one tool.
products.description:
The MultiQuick 7 is a three-in-one set that combines an immersion blender with a food processor attachment and other accessories, priced $50 to $100. It comes from Braun, a brand known for hand blenders.

It ranks first because the accessories turn a soup tool into a small prep station. Chopping onions or nuts with the processor attachment spares you from owning a second appliance. The tradeoff is storage: more parts mean more to wash and keep track of, and the listing does not give a wattage figure to compare against the others here.

Buy it if you want one gadget to handle soup, sauces and chopping. Skip it if you only blend soup and want the smallest, easiest kit.
cons: More parts to wash and store
products.idealFor: Home cooks who want one tool for several jobs.
products.skipIf: You only want a simple stick blender.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick Vario 5 Hand Blender, 21-Speed, 500W
products.verdict: A 500W motor, 21 speeds and a turbo boost for gentle starts and strong finishes.
products.description:
The Vario 5 has a 500W motor, a 21-speed dial and a turbo boost, priced $50 to $100. The wide speed range is the headline, since it lets you start slow and avoid spraying hot liquid.

It ranks second because speed control is the feature that separates a pleasant stick blender from a messy one. With 21 steps, you can ease into a hot soup or pulse a pesto, then use turbo for a final push. It sits behind the MultiQuick 7 because it lacks that model's food processor attachment, and the listing is short on accessories.

It suits cooks who blend soups and sauces often. Skip it if you want chopping attachments.
products.idealFor: Regular soup and sauce makers who want control.
products.skipIf: You want a chopper or whisk bundle.

products.name: Braun MQ50001M Vario 21-Speed Hand Blender with EasyClick
products.verdict: Another 500W, 21-speed Braun with an EasyClick system for swapping parts quickly.
products.description:
The MQ50001M is a 500W, 21-speed hand blender with TurboBoost and EasyClick, priced $50 to $100. EasyClick refers to a quick-release way of attaching and removing the shaft and accessories.

It ranks third because it matches the Vario 5 on motor and speed, and adds the convenience of tool-free swaps. That helps when you move from blending to whisking mid-recipe. The reason it does not rank higher is that the two Vario models are close, and the listing does not spell out which accessories come in the box.

Choose it if you value fast attachment changes. Skip it if you want a bundle that is clearly listed.
products.idealFor: Cooks who change attachments during a recipe.
products.skipIf: You need a clearly listed accessory bundle.

products.name: Turelar Immersion Blender Handheld Corded, 1100W 5 in 1 Set
products.verdict: An 1100W five-in-one set at $25 to $50, with the most attachments for the least money.
products.description:
The Turelar is a corded 1100W five-in-one hand blender set with attachments, priced $25 to $50. It is the cheapest option in the ranking and carries the biggest motor figure on paper.

It ranks fourth because attachments and low cost are real strengths, but wattage on a lesser-known brand says little about long-term durability. Many budget sets save money on gearing and housing materials, so treat the motor number as a marketing figure and check the warranty. Against Braun you give up brand history for more accessories.

It is a good starter for a first apartment or a light user. Skip it if you want a brand with long support.
products.idealFor: First kitchens and light, occasional use.
products.skipIf: You want a long track record and support.

products.name: KitchenAid Variable Speed Corded Hand Blender KHBV83
products.verdict: A corded variable-speed hand blender with attachments from a familiar kitchen brand.
products.description:
The KHBV83 is a corded, variable-speed hand blender that comes with attachments, priced $50 to $100. KitchenAid is one of the best-known names in home kitchens.

It ranks fifth because the listing gives few numbers: there is no wattage or speed count to compare with Braun's 21 speeds. Variable speed, in general, means you control how hard the blade spins, which is helpful for starting low. The brand adds confidence about support and parts, but it does not offer a clear edge on spec.

It suits a buyer who prefers a mainstream brand and values matching kitchen equipment. Skip it if you want documented specs.
products.idealFor: Buyers who prefer a mainstream kitchen brand.
products.skipIf: You want clear wattage and speed figures.

products.name: Braun MultiQuick 5 Hand Blender with Beaker and Whisk, 350W
products.verdict: A 350W dual-speed Braun with a beaker and whisk for basic jobs.
products.description:
The MultiQuick 5 is a 350W dual-speed hand blender with a beaker and a whisk, priced $50 to $100. It is the plainest Braun in the group.

It ranks sixth because dual speed is blunt compared with the 21-speed Varios, and the motor is the least powerful of the Brauns. Two speeds work for smoothies and mayonnaise but offer less finesse on hot soups. The beaker and whisk are handy extras that many cheaper sets omit.

It is a fair choice for occasional blending. Skip it if you want fine speed control.
products.idealFor: Occasional users who want a trusted brand.
products.skipIf: You want fine speed control for hot soups.

products.name: Cuisinart CSB-179 Smart Stick Variable Speed Hand Blender
products.verdict: A stainless steel, variable-speed stick blender from a long-standing kitchen brand.
products.description:
The CSB-179 Smart Stick is a stainless steel hand blender with variable speed, priced $50 to $100. It is a straightforward classic.

It ranks seventh because the listing contains no wattage, accessories or speed count. Variable speed is useful, and stainless steel suggests a sturdy shaft, but you are buying mostly on brand. It sits below the Braun units because they publish more details.

It works for someone who wants a simple, durable stick. Skip it if you want attachments or documented numbers.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want a no-frills stainless stick.
products.skipIf: You want attachments or published numbers.

products.name: Ninja Immersion Blender and Whisk CI201ND
products.verdict: A four-speed blender with a whisk and a 4oz cup in Deep Navy.
products.description:
The Ninja CI201ND is an immersion blender and whisk with four speeds and a 4oz cup, priced $50 to $100. It is a compact kit for small jobs.

It ranks last because the 4oz cup is small, which suits a sauce or a single drink but not a family batch. Four speeds offer more control than two but less than 21. The listing is short on motor details.

It suits small kitchens and single servings. Skip it if you cook for many people.
products.skipIf: You cook for several people at once.

methodology.title: Motor and Speed Range
methodology.description: We compared listed wattage and speed settings, with credit for fine control rather than raw power alone.

methodology.title: Attachments
methodology.description: Food processor, whisk, beaker and quick-release systems were scored on how much each kit can do.

methodology.title: Build and Brand
methodology.description: Shaft material, brand history and warranty clarity were used to judge durability on paper.

methodology.title: Ease of Use
methodology.description: Speed controls, parts count and cleanup were weighed for everyday convenience.

methodology.title: Value Under $100
methodology.description: Features were set against price brackets, with penalties for thin listings.

whatMatters.detail: Wattage affects how well a blender copes with thick mixtures, but it is not the whole story. A well-designed 500W Braun can beat a loosely engineered 1100W unit. Look at wattage alongside brand reputation and the speed range.

A wide range of speeds lets you start slowly to avoid splashing and finish fast for a smooth result. Braun's 21-speed models are at the top of this list for that reason. Check the listing for the speed count and for turbo boost.
A whisk, beaker or food processor extends what the blender can do. More parts also mean more washing and storage. Check which accessories are named in the listing and whether they are quick-release.

Stainless steel shafts resist stains and odours and handle hot liquids, while plastic shafts can stain from tomato sauces. Look for stainless wording on the listing. Check whether the shaft detaches for washing.

A hand blender is a modest purchase, but a motor that fails in a year is frustrating. Established brands generally offer clearer support. Read the warranty wording on the listing and check how replacement parts are handled.

howToChoose.intro: Start with how finely you want to control the blade.

cards.label: Variable speed
cards.text: A dial or trigger lets you ramp up gradually, which helps with hot soups and light sauces. The Braun Varios, the KitchenAid and the Cuisinart all use this approach.

cards.label: Fixed speeds
cards.text: Two or four preset speeds are simpler and cheaper. The Braun MultiQuick 5 and the Ninja use this, which suits quick smoothies and basic blending.

howToChoose.note: Variable speed is the better default because it lets you control splashing.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Fine speed control, a stainless shaft and enough motor power to run in a deep pot. A long shaft helps you reach the bottom without scorching your hand.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The Braun Vario 5 and the MQ50001M offer 21 speeds, and the Cuisinart CSB-179 adds a stainless build.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You blend several times a week or want a food processor attachment. The Braun MultiQuick 7 is worth the extra cost.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You blend occasionally. The Turelar set gives you a lot for little money.

faq.q: Can I use an immersion blender in a non-stick pot?
faq.a: It depends on the blade guard. A blade can scratch a non-stick surface if it touches the base. Tilt the blender slightly or use a guard if your model supplies one, and check the manual.

faq.q: What is the most common mistake when using one?
faq.a: Lifting the blender out of the liquid while it runs. That sprays hot soup across the kitchen. Keep the head submerged and switch off before lifting.

faq.q: Is the Braun MultiQuick 7 worth it over the Vario 5?
faq.a: It is if you will use the food processor attachment. If you only blend soup, the Vario 5 has finer speed control and fewer parts. Pick by what you actually cook.

faq.q: How do I clean a hand blender?
faq.a: Run the shaft in warm soapy water for a few seconds, rinse and dry it. Detach the shaft if it is removable, but never submerge the motor body. Wash attachments by hand unless the manual says otherwise.
Not necessarily. Blade design and speed control matter as much as wattage. The 1100W Turelar looks strong on paper, but the 500W Brauns have a stronger brand record.

faq.q: Can an immersion blender crush ice?
faq.a: Some can handle ice in small amounts, but it is hard on the blade and motor. Check the manual for guidance. A countertop blender is the better tool for frozen drinks.

finalTake: Buy the Braun MultiQuick 7 if you want one tool to blend and chop, and the Braun Vario 5 if soups and sauces are your main use. The MQ50001M adds quick-change attachments, the Turelar is the cheap bundle, and the KitchenAid suits brand loyalists. Choose variable speed whenever possible.
